title: Painting Exterior Trim and Shutters That Last
description: Exterior trim, doors, and shutters fail before siding does. How to prep, prime, caulk, and coat them for maximum life in Florida sun and rain.
h1: Painting Trim and Shutters: A Durability-First Approach
heroIntro: Trim and shutters take more sun, water, and handling than any other part of the exterior. They deserve tougher prep and a harder-wearing product than the siding.
excerpt: Exterior trim and shutters fail before the siding does. How to prep, prime, caulk, and coat them so they last in Florida weather.

secondary: how often to paint exterior trim
questions: What is the best paint for exterior trim in Florida?
Why does trim paint peel before siding?
Should shutters be removed before painting?

body: On a typical house, the first paint failures appear on window sills, door bottoms, fascia ends, and shutter edges, long before the siding looks tired. There are three reasons.

First, edges and corners are where paint film is thinnest. Paint pulls away from sharp edges as it dries, leaving less protection exactly where water runs off. Second, horizontal surfaces such as sills and the tops of rails hold water after every storm, and wood that wets and dries repeatedly swells and shrinks, cracking the paint and the caulk. Third, trim takes the most physical wear: doors are opened, railings are touched, and shutters flex in the wind. In North Central Florida, add intense sun on south and west faces, and trim can need attention years before the body.
Painting over a problem only hides it for a season. Walk the house with a screwdriver and a notepad.
bullets: Probe sills, the bottoms of door casings, fascia ends, and shutter rails. If the screwdriver sinks in easily, the wood is rotting and must be repaired or replaced.
Look for open joints where trim pieces meet, and gaps between trim and siding.
Check for bare wood, cracking, and alligatoring, all signs that the old coating has failed.
Note shutters that are loose or have broken louvers; it is easier to fix them while they are down.
If the home was built before 1978, test the trim paint for lead before scraping or sanding, and use lead-safe practices if it is positive.

body: Most of the life of a trim paint job is decided before the first coat of color. A careful prep sequence looks like this:
bullets: Wash to remove dirt, chalk, and mildew, then let the wood dry fully. A moisture meter helps on sills and fascia.
Scrape loose paint and feather-sand the edges so the transition will not show.
Replace rotted sections with new wood or a composite trim board, primed on all sides and the ends before installation.
Spot-prime every bare area with an exterior primer suited to the substrate. Bare wood left unprimed is the most common cause of early peeling.

Caulk every joint with a quality exterior sealant: trim-to-siding, miters, butt joints, and nail holes. Do not caulk the bottom edge of lap siding or the drip edge of a sill, where water needs to escape.

body: Trim and doors need a harder, more abrasion-resistant film than siding. Good options include premium 100% acrylic exterior trim paints and waterborne urethane-modified enamels, which dry hard, resist blocking (sticking) on doors and windows, and hold their gloss in UV. A semi-gloss or satin sheen sheds water better and cleans more easily than flat.

Apply two full coats, brushing or back-brushing so the paint is worked into the grain and onto edges. On shutters, spraying followed by back-brushing helps get coating into louvers without runs. Pay attention to the bottom edges of doors and shutters, which are often missed and are where water gets in.

Timing matters as much as product. Paint trim when the surface is dry and shaded, after the morning dew has burned off, and stop early enough that the film can set before the afternoon storms that roll through most Florida summer days. Painting a sill in direct midday sun makes the paint skin over too quickly, which traps solvent, causes lap marks, and weakens adhesion. Check the label for the minimum temperature and the recoat window, and do not rush the second coat; applying it before the first has dried can wrinkle the film.

sections.h2: Shutters: remove or paint in place?
body: Removing shutters gives better results. You can paint all sides, including the back and edges, which protects against moisture and lets you paint the siding behind them. Lay them flat on sawhorses, clean them, prime bare spots, and coat both faces.

Vinyl shutters can be painted if you use a paint rated for vinyl and stay within the color range the manufacturer recommends; very dark colors can cause vinyl to warp in Florida sun. Wood shutters need the same prep as other trim. Before rehanging, check the fasteners and replace corroded ones.

Decorative shutters screwed directly into stucco or siding can trap water behind them. When you rehang them, seal the fastener holes and consider small spacers so air can move behind the shutter and the wall can dry after rain.

Front doors are often the place to use a bold color, but dark colors absorb heat, and a dark door in direct afternoon sun can get hot enough to soften paint or stress weatherstripping. Check with the door manufacturer about dark colors on fiberglass or steel doors with full sun exposure. Leave doors open for a few hours after painting, and avoid closing them firmly for the first day or two to prevent the paint from sticking to the weatherstripping.
For color direction, our guide to historic paint colors in Gainesville shows how trim colors work on older homes, and our color consultation service helps put the whole scheme together.

sections.h2: Maintenance and when to call a pro
body: Recoat trim on a shorter cycle than the body of the house. Washing trim during the yearly house wash, checking caulk each fall, and touching up sills and door bottoms as soon as you see wear prevent wood rot, which is far more expensive than paint. Our article on cracked paint on window frames explains what happens when those warning signs are ignored.

Ground-floor trim and a front door are manageable DIY projects. Second-story fascia, rotten wood, and full exterior trim jobs are better handled by a professional crew. faqs.q: What sheen is best for exterior trim?
faqs.a: Semi-gloss or satin is best for most exterior trim. These sheens shed water, resist dirt, and clean easily, while still looking good next to a flatter siding finish.

faqs.q: How often should exterior trim be repainted in Florida?
faqs.a: Trim usually needs attention sooner than siding, especially on sunny sides and horizontal surfaces. Inspect it yearly and touch up or recoat as soon as you see cracking, peeling, or bare wood.

faqs.q: Can I paint over rotten trim?
faqs.a: No. Paint will not stop rot and will fail quickly over soft wood. Rotten sections should be cut out and replaced with primed wood or composite trim before painting.
Yes, with a paint formulated for vinyl and after thorough cleaning. Avoid colors much darker than the original, since dark colors can make vinyl overheat and warp in strong sun.
